video_title: What Will Determine the Durability of the AI Investment Cycle?
transcript: Recent AI-related stresses in equity  and credit markets and new regulatory   uncertainty following the US midterm  elections are raising fresh doubts about   the durability of the AI investment  cycle. So, just how durable is it,   what could cause it to inflect, and what would  a slowdown mean for companies and markets?   I'm Allison Nathan, and this  is Goldman Sachs Exchanges.   Each month, I speak with investors,  policymakers, and academics about the   most pressing, market-moving issues for our Top  of Mind report from Goldman Sachs Research.   For our latest edition, I spoke with Chamath  Palihapitiya, founder and CEO of Social Capital,   and Eric Sheridan, lead US?Internet  research analyst at Goldman Sachs.   I started by asking Chamath about an area of  the AI ecosystem under substantial pressure:   neoclouds. He explains that their  fundamental vulnerability is a   business model that ultimately depends on  large companies seeing meaningful returns   on their AI spend, which has yet to happen. Chamath, your recent worries about neoclouds   got a lot of attention. So, what were you  seeing that you think others were missing?   What's happening right now for me, Allison, is  I'm refining my point of view. Now, let me give   you where my sources of information come from. So, from 2015 to basically a year ago, most of my   investment was building this AI chip company, this  inference company called Groq, but about a year   before I moved up the stack and down the stack. And the reason was when I looked at the AI stack   in general, the binding constraint was  clearly moving to power. And so I spent a   lot of time ramping up an investment program  in land, power, and shell, and understanding   that whole ecosystem of literally the wildcatters  taking powered land, converting them to assets.   And then at the top, I started this  company called 8090 because I wanted   to understand the translation of AI into actual  ROI because I wasn't sure that I was seeing it,   and I wanted to make sure it was. So all  of this comes from those two insights.   And the single thing that I noticed is the hardest  problem with AI is the change management. And   so what happens is you go with these really  great broad sweeping ideas and productivity   is going to triple, profitability is going to  quadruple, and the lived reality is not that.   The lived reality is these projects are really  hard to implement. A lot of people in the middle   ranks of these companies are slightly skeptical to  afraid, and so they push back. So the diffusion of   this stuff is a lot slower than we thought it  would be. And then this other thing happens,   which is even if you have productivity gains,  they get lost in other parts of the value chain.   Meaning it's not like the person that saves two  hours a day is now doing two hours more things.   And so this is why actual factor productivity  is not really there. And then as a result,   this is why the ROI is not there in terms  of the EPS of the reporting companies.   I don't know how many companies you've seen  which are like, "EPS gains are a result of   buybacks." I've seen that. Profitability gains  have been because we have pricing power because   of inflation. I've seen that. How many companies  do you know that have said it's because of AI?   It's a relatively small universe. So it's almost  nonexistent, in my opinion. So that fact pattern   was bothering me. Then working inside this  company that I started with my co-founder,   we've accumulated six gigawatts now of  powered assets inside of the United States.   And the complexity, Allison, of getting  this turned on is mind-numbing. Mineral   rights in Texas, environmental studies because  there's some cesspool pit on the ground. The   concrete pads don't fit. The turbine guys are  backlogged. And you put it all together and the   lived experience was very concerning to me. And so when I looked at that, what I saw   is that there was a lot of promises on the  amount of capacity that would be available,   and the actual delivery volume was low, and then  the surface area for ROI was even lower still.   So this is just connecting these dots. That's  where I started to get concerned and just ask   the question, "how is the market going to react  to this?" And the market had already sniffed   this out because that's when the spreads  blew out, that's when the CDS blew out.   Chamanth, why does this mismatch between  promised capacity, actual capacity,   and ROI matter so much for neoclouds? Neoclouds are basically like the opposite   of a bank. So if you think about a bank, they  have short-term assets that they're getting from   customers that are depositing money that they  could pull in a second, so they're basically   borrowing short and they're lending long. They're lending in 10, 11-year duration in   mortgages and business loans. The neoclouds  are flipping that on its head. Their revenue   is very much speculative short-term revenue, but  their obligations are long-dated and fixed.   The best analogy that I've seen is one that  Ken Griffin and then Sridhar Ramaswamy,   who's the CEO of Snowflake, made, which  is the similarity to the airline industry,   which is you're buying these massive, fixed  assets. You're going into the ABS pool to   finance these things. The GPUs, using the airline  analogy, is like the engine. The shell of the   airplane is like the data center. The seats are  what all these companies are buying literally on   a per hour basis. The perishability  of the inventory is quite similar.   And then you have the folks like us who own  the binding constraints, which is you can have   a trillion billion planes, but if you don't  have airports where you are zoned to land,   it doesn't matter. Similarly, if you don't  have the powered land to actually build the   places where you can facilitate these things,  running these businesses are not viable.   So when I started to look at all of the flow of  funds, the setup is essentially a utilization one,   where you have the boundary conditions, and I'm  not saying it exists right now, but you have the   boundary conditions for a utilization mismatch. So, in the airline industry, what do we know? We   know that planes have to run between  80% to 85% utilized to break even,   and the margin and the earnings happen between  85% and call it 100% theoretical maximum.   What we know equivalently inside of neoclouds  is that the utilization ratio is about,   call it 70% to 75%. It waves depending on  the GPU class and depending on the neocloud,   but that's roughly. So you have the upper 25% as  where you can actually make money. So then you   have to think through, okay, what is happening  that allows them to make more or less money?   Well, number one is you have silicon efficiency,  but the problem is you can't take advantage of   silicon efficiency necessarily because you  have these upgrade cycles. And if you've made   long-dated commitments, $40, $50 billion dollar  packages to buy a certain class of silicon,   when that silicon gets upgraded next  year, which will automatically happen.   Beause NVIDIA is on a yearly cycle of just showing  you better and better stuff. You don't necessarily   upgrade. You have a six, seven, eight-year  window where you have to amortize this stuff.   You also have model efficiency happening.  So the big models, which are very expensive,   are shrinking in size, but they're  performing as the bigger ones. So   now you have better throughput. So, all of  these factors need to get factored in.   So you need demand to basically outstrip  all of that so that then you can take   the next generation of silicon. The bull case for the neoclouds   is that we start to show meaningful ROI  in the end customer, consumption of AI.   And it has to happen in the big companies. So, if you see the ROI, all the big companies   will spend more. You'll see a bunch of companies  move up and negatively churn into spending tens   of millions of dollars. That means that  token consumption will go off the charts.   That means utilization will go off the charts. Then the neoclouds print, the hyperscalers print,   NVIDIA prints, Micron prints, the foundational  models print. So, I think the bull case is   very obvious. But again, I think it's singularly  levered to ROI from the large paying customers   The bear case is actually a lot of the status  quo, meaning nothing needs to get much worse.   If things just stay where they are and the bulk  of the revenue distribution is more concentrated   in the hundreds of thousands to low millions  of dollars, what do we know? Well, I think we   can intuit that right now it's still very much  in an experimental bucket of most companies.   The status quo is budgets get instantiated,  but they don't move from experimentation   to hard run down the fairway. And  then in that case, what happens?   You don't have the explosion of token consumption,  which means you have utilization that stays in   this gray zone of 75% to 85%. And then  you have this utilization problem that   then catches up because you have a durational  mismatch of what you're paying and what you're   owing if you're a neocloud. So, I think this is the whole   game. I think in the next 18 months, the single  most important thing to probably look at is ROI   moves by the end-consuming companies. At least some organizations are now   using AI at scale. So why has meaningful  ROI yet to emerge even for these firms?   There's this weird thing happening where if  you graph, for example, agentic workflows, say   inside of 8090, what you see is token consumption  going up and agent loops going off the charts. So,   there's more agents inside my company doing  work by probably an order of magnitude than   humans. That's going up. But if you ask me,  what is your ROI of today versus yesterday.   Are you like 1% more profitable? I would say  probably not. In fact, I'm 1% less profitable   because I have more agents running more work  and it costs me more money in the aggregate,   even if the per cost token is going down. Now, by the way, this speaks to the other big   problem at the absolute end consumer of  these tokens, whether it's a global 2000   company or an individual. Using the internet  analogy, we are like in 1999. Why? In 1999,   the big behemoths, let's just say like Yahoo,  AOL, yeah, the purveyors of the internet,   their main business model was selling cost per  thousand ads. In 2026, the main purveyors of AI,   their business model, is selling cost per million  tokens. It's very similar. But three or four years   later, why did Google just completely dominate  the internet space until Meta came along? Because   they transitioned away from cost per thousand  ads to cost per acquisition or cost per click,   which is effectively saying we moved from buying  inventory to buying an outcome. We're sitting here   in 2026 still buying millions of tokens. Somebody  at scale will go to cost per outcome. And whoever   makes that transition will then rationalize  and allow businesspeople like me who actually   have a model that my finance team can show me and  say, hey, you spent a million dollars this month,   but here's what you generated, $1.5 million.  Great ROI, keep spending. I can't do that today.   So, the key question remains the same  one we ve been talking about for years:   Will AI capex generate sufficient returns? And  even if it does, will these returns become visible   before investors give up on the AI theme? To dig deeper into these questions I next   speak with Goldman Sachs' Eric Sheridan. Eric, the AI theme has dominated markets   over the last few years. But the  ongoing tech selloff suggests that   the market is increasingly questioning and  potentially losing confidence in the themes.   So are those concerns warranted or overblown? I typically don't try to qualify it as warranted   or overblown. I put it in a different category. I  would say they're understandable. We've been from   the excitement of the product side to the scaling  of the investment side to a natural evolution   into calling into question the return profile of  the investment side. Any compute cycle I've ever   analyzed goes through this process, historically  there is more scrutiny as you get deeper into the   cycle, and the investments build in the momentum.  And if there's a duration mismatch that emerges   between when you have to make the investment  versus the visibility as to when you're going   to earn a return on the investment, that's when  you typically will get some disillusionment   that makes its way into a cycle, and I  think we're very much in that period.   So, you don t think this time is different? No. Over the better part of the last 12 to 18   months, by my count, we've had three market  drawdowns against the AI theme at different   points in time that mostly, based on my investor  conversations, come down to visibility into how   linear things might be 18 or 24 months from  now. That typically is a return conversation,   and we're squarely in one right now. The  dollars have gone up and the end market   definition has gone up and we're further along  the cycle, which means the stakes go up.   And as the stakes go up, the  questions rise commensurate with it.   Eric, the timeline for visibility on returns  seems to be getting pushed further out with   each passing year. So is the market reaching  the limits of its patience at this point?   Visibility never seems to be happening as fast  as people want. But the hyperscaler businesses   had materially smaller backlogs of revenue  two and three years ago than they do now.   And some of these companies have disclosed in  public that 50% of their backlogs are going to   become revenue in the next two years. These things  typically happen over five to eight-year cycles,   cloud computing, mobile computing, desktop  computing. But typically, most people want   them to happen in six-month intervals. Investors want real-time capital allocation   to a forward compute curve. And that's just a  very unrealistic expectation. You have to build   ahead of the revenue dollars. It's almost like  investors want this to be real time inventory.   And that's not the way this works when you have  to build a data center, acquire land, fill it with   compute equipment, and then light it up and then  sell that compute to somebody else. In moments   of market distress or market drawdowns it never  seems to be happening as fast as people want.   But even as revenue backlogs have grown,  as you ve just said, capex has exploded,   which leaves revenue with an even higher wall  to climb. So, haven t the economics worsened?   The stakes have gone up. And there have been  some things that we wouldn't have foreseen,   like hyperinflation around memory pricing  or elements of input costs that have tracked   higher than we would've thought. That certainly  has been an area where we've been surprised.   You also have a friction point around monetization  on the consumer side and you have a friction point   on adoption on the enterprise side. It's a very  easy technology for consumers to adopt as long as   it is mostly being subsidized. It's a much slower  process for adoption on the enterprise side, you   have a rank-and-file employee in most enterprises  when you look at survey after survey who are   actually very reluctant to adopt AI because they  believe they're training their own replacement.   But in order to stand up the compute, you have to  spend the money. We've done work around return on   invested capital in the sector, anchoring around  what we would argue would be a bare minimum   return of 15% plus, and we believe hyperscalers  can very easily achieve a 15% plus return.   We ve made an assumption about the percentage of  the backlog that would have to turn into revenue   at a certain earnings margin or operating income  margin to generate a certain level of return. And   frankly, most people were positively surprised  that you wouldn't even have to approach 100%   of revenue backlog, let alone any further  growth from there to achieve a 15% return.   If I were to take estimates that 50% of their  backlogs are going to become revenue with no   conservatism as a point blank forecast from  companies like AWS and Amazon or Google Cloud   and Alphabet, my numbers would be materially  higher in their cloud division. So we have   some conservatism on the revenue side, and  by the way, last earnings period, you had   Microsoft and Amazon both give very detailed  ROIC answers. And you saw both stocks go up,   I think double digits on the back of their  earnings results. You had a comment from   Alphabet about return on invested capital  being well above their weighted average cost   of capital. You had Amazon giving a view that  they could grow 40% or more going forward.   Meta reported that they grew in the mid 20s when  12 months ago, I would have told you this quarter   they would have grown 12%. But instead, they're  growing in the mid-20s because the application   of AI in their core business is producing  more outcome of dollars for advertisers.   These are all pieces of the puzzle to gain  increased confidence in return on invested   capital. But I'm not sure everyone  is going to earn the same return,   right? Again, every compute cycle I've ever  covered, there's been winners and losers.   So, Eric, what do you believe is most likely to  precipitate a slowdown in the investment cycle?   People want me to answer this question based on  stock prices. It is not going to be a stock price   driven decision. The hyperscalers don't operate  that way. Their duration to absorb pain in their   stock prices is longer than the duration of most  investors I talk to day in and day out. This has   been true over any number of cycles. I remember  at one point when Meta was transitioning to short   form video and every investor on the planet  was like, he has to throw in the towel. He   didn't. And by the way, the stock absolutely  exploded to the upside when investors came   around to the longer duration view that Mark had. Three things would likely forestall or delay this   theme from playing out: demand, access to capital,  and access to power. We don't believe there's a   demand problem. By almost any measure across all  the TMT research we can do globally as a firm,   the demand signal actually is building  in momentum, not losing momentum. But if   there's a disruption in the demand curve,  you could find yourself in an overbuilt   situation. And companies would withdraw. A sustained disruption in the allocation of   capital behind the build out could, irrespective  of the demand, cause supply demand imbalance to   elongate and the folks who need the demand to meet  their financial obligations become under stress.   And supply coming online is an output of  can you build land power shell? The problem   is you can't scale energy as quickly as you  could scale land and shell and silicon. So,   you could find yourself short power, even though  the capital is available and the will to build   is there to actually light the compute up. If you start to weaken one of those three parts   of the puzzle, either the power's not there, the  capital's not there, or the demand's not there,   we will find ourselves in a more  permanent state as opposed to a   trough of disillusionment with the theme. So, while Eric is relatively optimistic,   he and Chamath both see ways that the investment  cycle could stall. I asked them who bears the risk   if that happens. Here is what Chamath had to say. Neoclouds have extremely well isolated SPVs,   special purpose vehicles. And they're relatively  well structured to minimize the risk.   So, then the question is how would we figure  out which neoclouds are at risk? Like what's   the frontier of risk amongst all of these things?  And this is where I've started to do this work   purely out of curiosity. I went through all the  regulatory filings of the hypers and all the   neoclouds that are public. You can do that. Feed  them all into AI and ask them to do the following,   which is look at all of the published regulatory  statements that they've made about buildout   capacity, where they are, and then marry that  against what their obligations are and how much   they've signed in take or pays. And you can net  it all out to an understanding of where they are   and actually being able to generate the revenue  needed to service their obligations. And you can   stack rank them from who's the most at risk to  who's the least at risk. And I just think it's an   exercise worth doing. And it's quite insightful. The other thing to think about is when you look at   the neos, if you're just a bunch of leases. You're  essentially a middleman. And I think that that   complicates your business model even further. You  need to have ownership of some of these critical   constraints because that will give you leverage.  And if you think about going into 2027 and 2028,   to the extent that AI continues to be a political  football and to the extent that folks are using   it as a way to protest their basket of issues,  and that it slows down data center development,   then owning these binding constraints has  enormous value. And so there are these Neos   that are aggressive owners of assets. I think  that's a very smart strategy. But then there   are others that are just leasers. And I think that  that's going to be highly problematic because then   you have to be absolutely operationally perfect. But the reality is that most SPVs are underpinned   by an IG wrapper somewhere. And these investment  grade wrappers are essentially guaranteeing some   downside protection and some rate of return to  the folks that have funded this and financed this.   And so all roads go back to the IGs that are the  funding source for this CapEx buildup, which are   the hyperscalers. And what's so interesting,  if you look at that dynamic is the big guys,   incredibly, have gone from massively cash flow  positive generally buying back stock, not issuing   debt, to massively free cash flow negative.  They are issuing debt. And interestingly now,   they're issuing equity to finance this thing.  So they've made an all-in bet that they can be   the backstop of this buildup because they  believe the AI bullcase. I think they are   going to be right. The question is when? And we went through this in the internet.   The internet unbelievably was right. All the  prognostications about the internet were right,   all the productivity gains were right.  All the revenue gains were right,   but they were wrong about the timing. And we  went through a clearing process. From 2002,   I lived it till really, you know, 2007. And then  there was GFC. We really didn't start finding our   footing until 2010, 2011 as an industry. That's  a long time. I think that there's going to be   this bump in the road at some point because  you're just not going to get this timing right   all the time in all scenarios. But the hypers,  they're going to be fine. These are incredible   businesses with pristine balance sheets. Eric agrees that the hyperscalers remain   relatively well positioned to weather a  potential slowdown in the AI investment cycle.   The hyperscalers are not going to end up in  a very negative situation. They have strong   balance sheets and underlying businesses that  generate free cash flow away from the AI theme.   I would argue there's a lot more risk when you  go further out on the balance-sheet dynamic   and people that are much more dependent  on the AI theme playing out for a lot of   their incremental revenue than the hyperscalers. You could look at the multiples in the market as a   tell for that as well. If you look at who trades  at single digit low double digit EPS multiples   right now, it's because most institutional  investors have absolutely no idea if they're going   to grow revenue or it's going to collapse. So I  think the market has somewhat sniffed that out.   Lets leave it there. My thanks to  ?Chamath Palihapitiya and Eric Sheridan.   And thank you for listening to this  episode of Goldman Sachs Exchanges,   which was recorded in October and  November 2026. I m Allison Nathan.
